triage.name: Diabetic Eye Problems
triage.reason: Vision changes in a diabetic patient with a clear screening and exam-based diagnosis; limited but real interview findings.

review_issues: presentation: older format without SNOMED terms
exam: older format without SNOMED terms

demographics: More common in people with longer duration of diabetes; prevalence rises with years since diagnosis
More common in racial and ethnic minority groups with higher diabetes prevalence and less access to eye screening
More common in people with type 1 diabetes, who often develop retinopathy earlier in life

risk_factors.text: Long duration of diabetes (especially more than 10 years)
Pregnancy in a person with diabetes

social_history: Limited access to regular eye care

chief_complaints.text: I see spots or dark wavy strings floating in my vision
I have trouble seeing at night or in dim light
My vision changes a lot from day to day
I have a dark shadow over part of my vision, like a curtain
My eyes hurt and look red

hpi.onset: Usually gradual and painless; often no symptoms at all until the disease is advanced. Sudden onset suggests a complication such as vitreous hemorrhage or retinal detachment.
hpi.duration: Develops over years of diabetes; symptoms may be present for weeks to months before presentation, or noticed only on a routine eye exam.
hpi.progression: Slowly progressive blurring and floaters as retinal blood vessels leak and new vessels grow; can suddenly worsen with bleeding into the eye or macular swelling.
hpi.location: Both eyes, though one eye may be worse than the other
hpi.quality: Blurred or wavy vision, floaters, missing patches, or a curtain-like shadow
hpi.severity: Mild to severe; can progress to significant vision loss if untreated
hpi.timing: Often constant once present; floaters and flashes may come and go early on
aggravating: Straining or heavy lifting (can trigger bleeding)

associated_symptoms.text: Dark shadow or curtain over part of vision

atypical.how_it_differs: Diabetic retinopathy can worsen rapidly during pregnancy, and symptoms may appear earlier than expected; close monitoring is needed.
Symptoms may be attributed to aging or cataracts, and diabetic eye disease may be discovered only on routine exam.
Children with type 1 diabetes rarely have retinopathy before puberty or within the first few years of diagnosis, but it can occur if diabetes is long-standing and poorly controlled.

general.mild: Well-appearing, no distress; may have no visual complaints at all
general.moderate: Well-appearing but reports or shows reduced central vision; no eye redness or pain
general.severe: Reduced vision affecting function; may squint or hold objects closer; no acute distress
general.critical: Marked vision loss or a new curtain-like visual field defect; may be anxious but not toxic

findings.maneuver: Check visual acuity in each eye separately with a Snellen chart (with correction)
findings.finding: Reduced best-corrected visual acuity, worse in one eye or both

findings.maneuver: Check visual acuity in each eye separately with a Snellen chart
findings.finding: Normal visual acuity, which does not exclude early retinopathy

findings.maneuver: Perform a dilated fundoscopic exam and look at the retinal periphery and posterior pole
findings.finding: Dot-and-blot hemorrhages, microaneurysms, hard exudates, or cotton-wool spots

findings.maneuver: On dilated fundoscopy, inspect the macula for thickening, exudates, or loss of the foveal light reflex
findings.finding: Retinal thickening or hard exudates at the macula, suggesting diabetic macular edema

findings.maneuver: On dilated fundoscopy, examine the optic disc, retinal vessels, and iris for new vessel growth
findings.finding: New vessels on the disc, elsewhere on the retina, or at the iris (rubeosis iridis)

findings.maneuver: On dilated fundoscopy, look for blood obscuring the retina; assess for a relative afferent pupillary defect
findings.finding: Blood in the vitreous obscuring retinal details, or a relative afferent pupillary defect

findings.maneuver: Measure intraocular pressure with a tonometer
findings.finding: Elevated intraocular pressure, suggesting neovascular glaucoma

findings.maneuver: Inspect the lens with a slit lamp or ophthalmoscope
Inspect the conjunctiva and sclera in room light
Ask about and assess for ocular pain on palpation or eye movement
Inspect the eyes from the front and above for proptosis or lid retraction
Test pupillary light reflexes and look for a relative afferent pupillary defect
findings.finding: Equal, reactive pupils without an afferent pupillary defect

findings.maneuver: Confrontational visual fields in each eye
findings.finding: Full visual fields without a curtain-like defect

findings.maneuver: Screen cranial nerves, strength, sensation, and coordination
Inspect the feet and test monofilament sensation and pedal pulses
findings.finding: Signs of peripheral neuropathy or peripheral arterial disease, reflecting microvascular complications

labs.caveat: Reflects glycemic control over the past 2-3 months; higher values track with retinopathy severity and progression.
Fasting glucose; hyperglycemia drives microvascular injury but a single value is less informative than HbA1c.
Diabetic nephropathy often coexists with retinopathy; renal function affects contrast and medication choices.
Hyperlipidemia is a modifiable risk factor for progression of diabetic eye disease.
Proteinuria suggests concurrent diabetic nephropathy, another microvascular complication.
Pregnancy can accelerate diabetic retinopathy; check in anyone who could be pregnant before planning imaging or treatment.

imaging.preferred_when: Screening and staging of diabetic retinopathy

findings.text: Venous beading and intraretinal microvascular abnormalities
Neovascularization of the disc or elsewhere

imaging.study: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the macula
imaging.preferred_when: Suspected diabetic macular edema or unexplained vision loss

findings.text: Retinal thickening with intraretinal cystoid spaces at the macula

imaging.preferred_when: When dye-based angiography is not available or is contraindicated

findings.text: Capillary nonperfusion and enlargement of the foveal avascular zone

imaging.preferred_when: Planning laser treatment or evaluating suspected neovascularization

findings.text: Diffuse or focal leakage at the macula
Tractional retinal detachment or posterior vitreous detachment

initial.why: Documents glycemic control, which drives retinopathy progression
Assesses renal function and electrolytes, relevant to coexisting nephropathy and treatment planning
Identifies a modifiable vascular risk factor
The primary diagnostic test; detects microaneurysms, hemorrhages, exudates, and neovascularization
Documents and stages retinopathy for monitoring and referral

confirmatory.test: Optical coherence tomography (OCT) of the macula
confirmatory.why: Confirms and quantifies diabetic macular edema when vision is reduced or the macula looks abnormal
Maps leaking vessels and neovascularization before laser or anti-VEGF treatment
confirmatory.only_if: neovascularization or macular edema is suspected and treatment is being planned

supporting.why: Screens for proteinuria suggesting concurrent diabetic nephropathy
Pregnancy can accelerate retinopathy and affects treatment choices
Evaluates the retina when vitreous hemorrhage prevents direct visualization

supporting.only_if: dye angiography is unavailable or contraindicated

not_indicated.why: No role in the diagnosis or staging of diabetic eye disease
Not indicated unless acute coronary syndrome is suspected
No role in vision loss from diabetic eye disease
Not useful; inflammatory markers do not diagnose diabetic retinopathy
Not indicated for isolated visual symptoms without focal neurologic findings

not_indicated.test: MRI brain with and without contrast
not_indicated.why: Not indicated unless a central neurologic cause of vision loss is suspected

decision_points: Any sudden floaters, flashes, curtain-like visual field loss, or vision loss needs urgent ophthalmology evaluation to exclude retinal detachment or vitreous hemorrhage
Pregnancy test before planning imaging or treatment in anyone who could be pregnant
Poorly controlled blood pressure and glucose should be addressed alongside eye treatment to slow progression

criteria.name: Diabetic retinopathy severity scale (ETDRS-based)
criteria.summary: Retinopathy is graded from no apparent retinopathy through mild, moderate, and severe nonproliferative stages to proliferative retinopathy, based on the number and extent of microaneurysms, hemorrhages, venous beading, and intraretinal microvascular abnormalities; diabetic macular edema is graded separately as present or absent and by central involvement.
items: Moderate nonproliferative: more than microaneurysms but less than severe
Severe nonproliferative: extensive hemorrhages in all four quadrants, venous beading in two or more quadrants, or intraretinal microvascular abnormalities in one or more quadrants
Diabetic macular edema graded separately by central involvement

differential.name: Retinal detachment
differential.why_considered: Sudden floaters, flashes of light, and a curtain-like shadow over part of the vision are classic for retinal detachment and can also occur with diabetic tractional detachment or vitreous hemorrhage.
differential.trigger: Sudden onset of flashes, a shower of floaters, or a curtain-like visual field defect

history: Abrupt onset over hours to days rather than gradual
Curtain or shade descending over the vision
Recent eye trauma or eye surgery
exam: Visual field defect corresponding to the detached retina
Retina visibly elevated or folded on dilated fundoscopy
imaging: B-scan ocular ultrasound showing a retinal membrane tethered to the optic disc
OCT showing separation of the neurosensory retina from the retinal pigment epithelium

differential.name: Acute angle-closure glaucoma
differential.why_considered: Diabetes raises the risk of glaucoma, and both can present with vision loss; acute angle closure is a sight-threatening emergency that must be excluded.
differential.trigger: Severe eye pain, headache, nausea and vomiting, red eye, and halos around lights

history: Sudden severe eye pain with headache and vomiting
Halos or colored rings around lights
Recent dim light exposure or use of anticholinergic medications
exam: Red, injected eye with a fixed mid-dilated pupil
Corneal haze and a hard eye on palpation
Markedly elevated intraocular pressure on tonometry
labs: No specific laboratory finding; diagnosis is clinical and tonometric

differential.name: Cataract
differential.why_considered: Painless, gradual blurring and glare are common in diabetes, and cataracts develop earlier and faster in people with diabetes.

history: Slowly progressive blurring and glare, especially at night
exam: Cloudy or opacified lens on slit lamp examination
Reduced visual acuity that improves with refraction or pinhole

differential.name: Hypertensive retinopathy
differential.why_considered: Hypertension commonly coexists with diabetes and produces retinal hemorrhages, exudates, and cotton-wool spots that can mimic diabetic retinopathy.

history: Headaches or visual symptoms in the setting of very high blood pressure
exam: Arteriolar narrowing, arteriovenous nicking, and flame hemorrhages
Absence of microaneurysms, which are the hallmark of diabetic retinopathy
labs: Renal function abnormalities suggesting hypertensive end-organ damage

differential.name: Central retinal vein occlusion
differential.why_considered: Sudden painless vision loss with retinal hemorrhages in a patient with diabetes and vascular risk factors.

history: Sudden painless loss of vision in one eye
Often in older patients with hypertension or glaucoma
exam: Diffuse flame hemorrhages in all four quadrants ('blood and thunder' fundus)
imaging: Fluorescein angiography showing delayed venous filling and widespread leakage

differential.name: Vitreous hemorrhage from other causes
differential.why_considered: Sudden floaters and vision loss from blood in the vitreous can occur with diabetic proliferative retinopathy but also from trauma, retinal tear, or other vascular disease.

history: Sudden onset of floaters or vision loss
Recent eye trauma or eye surgery
Known bleeding disorder or anticoagulant use
exam: Blood obscuring the retina on fundoscopy
Relative afferent pupillary defect if severe
imaging: B-scan ocular ultrasound showing vitreous opacities and assessing for retinal detachment

differential.name: Age-related macular degeneration
differential.why_considered: Central vision loss with drusen and pigmentary changes in older adults can resemble diabetic macular edema.

history: No history of diabetes or long-standing diabetes
exam: Drusen, pigmentary changes, or geographic atrophy at the macula
imaging: OCT showing drusen, subretinal fluid, or choroidal neovascular membrane
Fluorescein angiography showing choroidal neovascular leakage

severity.mild: No apparent or mild nonproliferative retinopathy; normal or near-normal visual acuity; no macular edema; asymptomatic
severity.moderate: Moderate nonproliferative retinopathy or non-center-involving diabetic macular edema; mild to moderate blurring or floaters; vision still functional
severity.severe: Severe nonproliferative or proliferative retinopathy, center-involving macular edema, or vitreous hemorrhage; significant vision loss affecting daily activities
severity.critical: Not applicable; diabetic eye disease itself is not immediately life-threatening, though sudden severe vision loss requires urgent ophthalmology evaluation

red_flags.finding: Sudden shower of new floaters or flashes of light
red_flags.meaning: Possible vitreous hemorrhage or retinal tear/detachment; needs urgent ophthalmology evaluation

red_flags.finding: Curtain-like shadow or dark shadow over part of the vision
Sudden painless vision loss in one eye
red_flags.meaning: Vitreous hemorrhage, retinal detachment, or vascular occlusion; urgent evaluation needed

red_flags.finding: Severe eye pain with redness, headache, nausea, and halos around lights
red_flags.meaning: Possible acute angle-closure glaucoma or neovascular glaucoma; sight-threatening emergency

red_flags.finding: New vessels on the iris (rubeosis iridis) or elevated intraocular pressure
red_flags.meaning: Neovascular glaucoma; requires urgent treatment to prevent irreversible vision loss

complications.name: Diabetic macular edema
clues: Hard exudates or retinal thickening at the macula on fundoscopy

complications.name: Vitreous hemorrhage
clues: Blood obscuring the retina on fundoscopy

complications.name: Tractional retinal detachment
clues: Retina elevated or folded on ultrasound

complications.name: Cataract
clues: Cloudy lens on slit lamp examination

special_populations.differences: Diabetic retinopathy can worsen rapidly during pregnancy; screening and monitoring should be more frequent, and treatment may be needed earlier.
Symptoms may be attributed to aging or cataracts; diabetic eye disease may be found only on routine dilated eye examination.

Children with type 1 diabetes rarely develop retinopathy before puberty or within the first few years of diagnosis, but it can occur with long-standing poorly controlled diabetes; screening begins after puberty or 5 years of diabetes.
The underlying condition itself; duration of diabetes and glycemic control are the strongest predictors of retinopathy progression.

key_questions.question: How long have you had diabetes, and what type?
key_questions.looking_for: Long duration (especially more than 10 years) and type 1 diabetes, both of which raise the risk of retinopathy

key_questions.question: What is your vision like now compared with before, and is it blurry, wavy, or missing patches?
key_questions.looking_for: Gradual painless blurring or wavy central vision suggesting macular edema

key_questions.question: Do you see new spots or dark wavy strings floating in your vision?
key_questions.looking_for: Floaters, which suggest vitreous hemorrhage or retinal tear

key_questions.question: Have you noticed flashes of light or a dark shadow like a curtain over part of your vision?
key_questions.looking_for: Flashes or a curtain-like defect, which suggest retinal detachment and need urgent ophthalmology evaluation

key_questions.question: When was your last dilated eye exam?
key_questions.looking_for: No recent screening; early retinopathy is usually asymptomatic and found only on dilated exam

key_questions.question: What have your blood sugar and HbA1c readings been like lately?
key_questions.looking_for: Poor glycemic control, which drives retinopathy progression

key_questions.question: How well controlled is your blood pressure, and do you take medication for it?
key_questions.looking_for: Uncontrolled hypertension, a strong modifiable risk factor

key_questions.question: Do you have high cholesterol, and are you on a statin?
key_questions.looking_for: Hyperlipidemia, another modifiable vascular risk factor

key_questions.question: Do you smoke or use tobacco?
key_questions.looking_for: Tobacco use, which raises the risk of progression

key_questions.question: Does your vision change a lot from day to day, or do you have trouble seeing colors?
key_questions.looking_for: Fluctuating vision and color difficulty, which occur with diabetic eye disease

key_questions.question: Do you have eye pain, redness, or halos around lights?
key_questions.looking_for: Pain, redness, or halos, which suggest acute angle-closure or neovascular glaucoma rather than retinopathy

key_questions.question: Could you be pregnant? When was your last period?
key_questions.looking_for: Pregnancy, which can accelerate retinopathy and affects treatment choices

key_questions.question: Have you had any recent eye trauma, eye surgery, or bleeding problems?
key_questions.looking_for: Other causes of vitreous hemorrhage or retinal detachment

reasoning_points: Long-standing diabetes with poor glycemic control and hypertension as the main risk factors
Gradual painless blurring, floaters, or fluctuating vision in a patient with diabetes
Dilated fundoscopic exam showing microaneurysms, dot-and-blot hemorrhages, hard exudates, or cotton-wool spots
Macular thickening or exudates explaining reduced central vision (diabetic macular edema)
Neovascularization or vitreous hemorrhage indicating proliferative disease
Red flags such as flashes, a curtain-like shadow, or sudden vision loss prompting urgent ophthalmology referral
Pregnancy, blood pressure, and lipid control considered because they modify progression and treatment
Look-alikes such as retinal detachment, acute angle-closure glaucoma, cataract, and hypertensive retinopathy excluded

easy: Long-standing diabetes with classic floaters and blurred vision
Dilated fundoscopy shows microaneurysms and dot-and-blot hemorrhages
medium: Asymptomatic patient found only on routine dilated screening exam
Reduced central vision with macular edema on OCT
Vision changes attributed to aging or cataract in an older adult
Coexisting diabetic nephropathy or neuropathy suggesting microvascular disease
hard: Sudden floaters and vision loss from vitreous hemorrhage obscuring the retina
Curtain-like visual field defect suggesting tractional retinal detachment
Pregnant patient with rapidly worsening retinopathy
Eye pain and redness with elevated pressure suggesting neovascular glaucoma
Normal visual acuity despite significant retinopathy
